summary:
Indonesia is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, this provision effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations, and reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women in addition to the national morality provisions. In Aceh, where Sharia law applies, two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025; those penalties are imposed under provincial religious law and reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors. Enforcement elsewhere in the republic also takes the form of venue raids: on 22 June 2025 Indonesian police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a "gay party" and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman, an operation Amnesty International described as a blatant violation of human rights and privacy that broke no law.

No Riau-specific statute, raid, arrest, protection mechanism or service record appears in the sourced material, and the Riau province article carries no provincial divergence from the national position. A visitor to Riau therefore stands under the national framework: private consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised in most of the republic, but Indonesia provides no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protections on the grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and legal gender change on official documents requires sex-reassignment surgery plus a judge's approval.

Official policy now frames LGBTQ+ people as a security matter. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 lists nonmilitary threats and places LGBTQ+ people, including "the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture", within national defence policy as risks to be monitored and controlled alongside terrorism and narcotics. Reporting from August 2026 ties that framing to a wave of vigilante mob attacks on transgender women during 14-16 July 2026, including in West Java's Bogor, as the government moves to codify anti-LGBTQ+ attitudes into law; commentators quoted by ABC News state that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy.

There is a directly documented death of a trans traveller in Indonesian custody. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in Bali in 2022. His mother in Lima was told during a WhatsApp call that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody; his mother alleges that police beat him, while Indonesian police have denied that violence was used.

Charges under anti-LGBT provisions can be severe. In August 2025 police arrested three men over an alleged LGBTQ Facebook community page, with up to 12 years' imprisonment possible if convicted.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement documented in Indonesia targets gatherings and moral offences rather than transgender identity as such: the June 2025 villa operation was launched after public reports of a party, and the February 2025 caning followed a relationship rather than a person's presentation. A trans visitor who avoids organised events and nightlife settings is not, on the sourced record, the ordinary object of police attention, but the same sources show that crowds and complaints, not formal charges, initiate the risk.

The mob violence of 14-16 July 2026 is recorded in West Java's Bogor, not in Riau, and the two provinces with explicit statutory criminalisation of same-sex activity, Aceh and South Sumatra, are also outside Riau. Riau is thus comparatively less exposed than those provinces while remaining subject to the same national penal code, the same absence of protective legislation and the same official framing of LGBTQ+ people as a security threat.

Custody risk is documented at the level of the state rather than any single province. The 2022 death of Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla followed an airport arrest on drug charges and involved an alleged extortion demand, so drug-related detention is a distinct hazard for any traveller, trans or otherwise.
localsOnly:
Legal gender change for residents of Riau follows the national requirement: sex-reassignment surgery plus a judge's approval are needed before a marker on official documents can be amended. Nothing in the sourced material records a Riau-specific procedure, a provincial dispensation or a provincial obstacle to that process.

Residents of Riau have no statutory recourse on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. Indonesia provides no anti-discrimination law and no hate-crime protection covering these characteristics, and the sourced material documents no Riau provincial ordinance filling that gap.

The national penal code applies to residents on the same terms as to visitors, and residents travelling to Aceh place themselves under provincial Sharia penalties that apply to anyone present there. Reporting indicates that prosecutions under the extra-marital sex provision are selective rather than systematic, and no record of prosecutions originating in Riau appears in the sourced material.

The October 2025 presidential decree placing LGBTQ+ people within national defence policy binds the whole republic, including Riau's own security and civil agencies. No Riau-specific implementation directive, task force or monitoring arrangement is documented in the material reviewed.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the national penal code or the August 2025 Facebook-page charges have been enforced by courts in Riau is unresolved: the sourced material contains no Riau court record, arrest report or provincial police statement, and the Riau province reference article carries no usable finding.

Entry and exit practice is not sourced. Nothing reviewed addresses visa screening, airport or land-border processing, or the treatment of passports carrying an amended gender marker on arrival in Indonesia or at Riau's own ports of entry.

Access to gender-affirming care, legal assistance and support organisations inside Riau is not sourced. No clinic, NGO, hotline or shelter record for the province appears in the material, and the absence of such records should not be read as evidence that none exist.

One source in the inventory is a wire report retrieved only as a fetch-time summary, so the detail of the police account in the 2022 custody death rests on partial retrieval. The claim that prosecutions under the extra-marital sex provision are selective rather than systematic comes from reporting rather than from conviction data, which the material does not provide.
